newsitem.title: FRANCE: France urges U.S. to end "snub" incident.
newsitem.headline: France urges U.S. to end "snub" incident.

text.p: France urged the U.S. State Department on Thursday to put an end to a simmering dispute over a purported but denied snub to Secretary of State Warren Christopher by French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

"Mr de Charette and Mr Christopher had already agreed in Washington (on Monday) to ask their aides to stop making statements about this affair," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters.

"I think we should let this affair, which is now over a week old, go away," Doutriaux said. "I will make no further comment about it and I hope (State Deparment spokesman Nicholas) Burns will do the same," he said.
Doutriaux was commenting on a statement attributed to Burns in Washington on Wednesday reasserting that the United States considered de Charette had indeed snubbed Christopher.

The French minister referred to the controversy himself on Wednesday, when he said in response to a parliamentary question: "It was a grotesque incident but it was entirely manipulated by American circles who were at its origin."
The dispute initially arose when U.S. officials accused de Charette of walking out during a toast in honour of Christopher at a NATO function in Brussels earlier this month.

The French minister's office said he had not meant to snub Christopher and a French official said he had left to hold a news conference because he did not know a tribute to the secretary of state was planned.

A senior Socialist opposition politician, former defence minister Paul Quiles, poured scorn on de Charette in parliament on Wednesday, saying his prestige was "in tatters" and France had become an object of international ridicule.

The daily Le Figaro, close to the Paris government, quoted unidentified diplomatic sources as saying France believed Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs John Kornblum had initiated the dispute, instructing Burns to leak the "snub" story.
The alleged snub in Brussels followed a series of disputes between Paris and Washington including the question of who should hold NATO's southern command based in Naples.
